ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Intensely pruritic, red, sore rash for ~4 days; seeking quick relief.
- Symptoms: Itch is severe (disrupts sleep and concentration), skin is dry and cracked in places; no pus, no bleeding. Distribution: chest, hands, and inside elbows (antecubital fossae); no face involvement. Patient showers daily which temporarily eases itch. OTC topical steroid used last night without relief yet; prior antihistamines provided little/no benefit. No fever, no respiratory or urinary symptoms, no GI symptoms reported. No clear trigger identified; he hiked last weekend.
- Past medical history: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) previously; past asthma (resolved). No other chronic conditions mentioned.
- Medications/allergies: No regular meds. Tried OTC steroid cream recently; has used prescribed topical steroids and bath emollients in the past. Tried OTC antihistamines recently without benefit. No known allergies.
- Family/social history: 31-year-old; lives with flatmates; works as a project manager at a pharmaceutical company; nonsmoker; drinks a few beers per week; enjoys hiking.
- Vital signs/exam findings: No vitals provided. Remote/video impression by clinician: rash "appears familiar" (suggestive of eczema); clinician mentioned chest and back involvement (patient emphasized chest, hands, and inside elbows). Skin described by patient as dry and cracked; no signs of infection reported.
- Labs/imaging: None mentioned.

I: Scabies infestation: Sudden, severe generalized pruritus (worse at night with sleep disturbance), hand involvement, shared living situation with flatmates; steroids/antihistamines often minimally helpful.
Dermatophyte infection (tinea corporis/manuum): Pruritic, scaly rash can involve trunk/hands; may be confused with eczema, though usually subacute and annular.
N: Cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides): Chronic pruritic patches/plaques; atypical here due to very acute 4‑day onset and age 31, but can mimic eczema.
D: Asteatotic (xerotic) eczema: Barrier dysfunction with dry, cracked, very itchy skin; flares in dry environments; aligns with dry/cracked description.
I2: Drug-induced morbilliform eruption: Acute pruritic rash after new medication exposure; less likely as patient denies new meds.
Irritant contact dermatitis (e.g., soaps/detergents/sanitizers): Hand/chest involvement possible; showers provide transient relief; no clear product change reported.
A: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare: Prior history; flexural (antecubital) and hand involvement; intense itch and xerosis with fissuring; no systemic symptoms.

Allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., plant/rhus, fragrances, preservatives, occupational exposures): Acute intensely pruritic dermatitis after possible outdoor exposure (hiking) or work-related contact; chest/hands distribution plausible.
Urticaria: Acute pruritic eruption possibly from allergen exposure; less consistent with persistent cracked skin and poor antihistamine response.
T: Photodermatitis/sunburn or photoallergic dermatitis: Chest and hand exposure during hiking could trigger acute pruritic erythema; typically more burning than cracking; distribution would favor sun-exposed areas.
E: Systemic pruritus due to endocrine/metabolic disease (e.g., thyroid, cholestasis, renal): Usually generalized itch without primary eczematous rash; less consistent with localized cracked dermatitis.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: History of eczema with classic distribution (flexural elbows, hands, trunk), severe pruritus, xerosis and fissuring, no systemic symptoms; acute flare plausible without an obvious trigger.

Acute onset severe itch involving hands and chest after recent hiking and possible environmental/occupational exposures; contactants could provoke widespread dermatitis even without recognized product changes.
Marked pruritus interfering with sleep, hand involvement, shared housing; steroids/antihistamines often unhelpful. Lack of classic signs does not exclude early or partially treated scabies.
Acute pruritic process could reflect hives; however, persistent sore/cracked skin and minimal antihistamine response argue against typical transient wheals.
Can cause itchy scaly plaques on trunk/hands; time course and description (no annular lesions) make it less likely than eczematous or contact dermatitis.

supporting_evidence: Distribution includes flexural (inside elbows) and hands, with trunk involvement
Skin described as dry and cracked (xerosis/fissuring)
Clinician impression that rash looked familiar for eczema
opposing_evidence: Distribution broader than prior episodes (now chest and hands)
OTC topical steroid and antihistamines provided little relief so far (though steroid used only 1 day)
Very acute onset following hiking raises possibility of contact or infestation

supporting_evidence: Hands and chest involved—sites commonly exposed to irritants/allergens (hands) or secondary transfer to chest
Recent hiking could imply plant allergen exposure; patient showers to ease itch
Works in pharmaceutical setting—possible occupational exposures
opposing_evidence: No classic linear vesicles or clear exposure pattern reported
Flexural (inside elbows) involvement can be less typical for pure contact dermatitis

supporting_evidence: Severe pruritus disturbing sleep (often worse at night in scabies)
Lives with flatmates (risk of spread/household cases)
Limited response to antihistamines and topical steroids
opposing_evidence: Very acute 4‑day onset (primary scabies often has longer incubation)
No reported burrows, interdigital web involvement, genital/beltline lesions
No known contacts with pruritus (patient hasn’t asked)
Patient describes persistent sore, cracked skin rather than transient wheals
Distribution includes chronic eczematous sites (flexures) rather than classic migratory wheals

supporting_evidence: Pruritic rash on trunk/hands can be fungal
Topical steroids can alter appearance and reduce inflammation without clearing fungus
opposing_evidence: Very acute 4‑day course atypical for tinea
No description of annular, leading scale borders or unilateral hand involvement
Multiple noncontiguous sites make primary tinea less likely
